The Beginning

From Code
to Command

I did not plan to become a project manager. I started by building things. But the more I coordinated teams, the more I realized: my strongest skill is not writing code. It is making sure the right people are building the right things, at the right time.
Nafiz Al Mahmud / 2025

It started as a Programmer Intern at the Survey of Bangladesh, Ministry of Defence, where I worked on national mapping systems. Working at that level taught me to take documentation and accuracy very seriously.

At Astrotech Technologies, I built backend systems and migrated old software to newer frameworks. That experience lets me talk clearly with developers , something most project managers cannot do.

At ARA Technologies, I coordinated government infrastructure projects for NESCO and DPDC , bringing together field teams, engineers, and documents across real construction sites.

Today at TechnoNext Software Ltd, I lead 7 software projects at the same time with a team of 20. Everything I do now is built on that full journey.

Chapter One / Present

My Story at
TechnoNext

Dec 2025 / Present / Project Coordinator

TechnoNext Software Ltd is a technology concern of US-Bangla Group, one of Bangladesh's most prominent conglomerates. It builds digital solutions for domestic and international markets across mobile applications and enterprise software.

Joining TechnoNext was the biggest challenge of my career. Seven projects running at the same time. Fifteen developers, five designers, and stakeholders from different departments all needing regular updates. The job was keeping everything moving without anything slipping.

This is where I grew from someone who follows a process into someone who designs one. Every sprint, every requirement document, every stakeholder meeting here has a real business outcome attached to it.

Chapter Two / Sept 2024 to Dec 2025

Ground Truth at
ARA Technologies

Before I ever ran a software standup, I was coordinating power grid projects for two of Bangladesh's biggest electricity companies. ARA put me at the crossroads of field engineering and project management , and that mix changed how I work forever.

The work was not just behind a screen. I was coordinating teams building real infrastructure on the ground. Jira tracked timelines. Google Earth Pro checked site conditions. Confluence kept design and construction aligned. ClickUp mapped dependencies. AutoCAD schematics were the backbone of every handoff.

Chapter Three / Jun 2024 to Sept 2024

The Technical
Foundation

June 2024 to September 2024
Astrotech Technologies
Junior Backend Developer

The role that gave me the technical vocabulary every project manager needs but rarely has.

PythonDjangoREST APIsMySQLAuthenticationSystem Migration

Most project managers do not know what it actually takes to build a feature. They know timelines and requirements , but not why a technical decision made today can slow down three sprints from now.

At Astrotech, I was the one writing the code. I built CRM backends, managed security protocols, and led system migrations without taking anything offline.

That experience did not make me a better developer. It made me a better project manager. When a developer tells me something is hard, I know how to tell the difference between a genuine technical challenge and a process problem I can fix. When I write a BRD, I know exactly how an engineer will read it.

CRM Backend Systems
Built and maintained backend systems for CRM applications serving real commercial users.
Security and Authentication
Set up encryption and login systems to keep sensitive user data safe in production.
Legacy Migration
Moved old systems to modern frameworks without disrupting live services.
API Development
Built REST APIs and database connections that linked frontend apps to backend services.
Chapter Four / March 2024 to June 2024

Where It
All Started

This story starts with an internship at the National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI), Ministry of Defence. The systems I worked on were national-level mapping infrastructure , the kind that other government systems depend on.

I helped test and maintain systems where a single missed bug had real consequences. Working with senior engineers on national infrastructure taught me one thing above all: bad documentation costs more than bad code.

No later job has taught me what this did: what it means to work when failure is simply not an option. That mindset has stayed with me through every project since.

How I Work

Agile in Practice

At TechnoNext I run Agile across 7 active projects with a team of 20. This is not theory , it is something I do every single day.

Phase 01
Sprint Planning
Turning requirements into clear sprint tasks with defined goals, acceptance criteria, and assigned owners. Every sprint starts with the whole team aligned on what success looks like.
Phase 02
Daily Execution
Running daily standups, watching progress metrics, and catching blockers early. The standup is not a status update , it is how we keep things moving.
Phase 03
Sprint Review
Showing stakeholders what got done each sprint , honestly, clearly, and tied to original goals. Every review is a chance to keep trust strong and sharpen the next sprint.
Phase 04
Retrospective
Taking feedback from the team and turning it into concrete changes. Good retrospectives make teams noticeably better sprint after sprint.
